Media controls and element state

Four ideas that came out of the parts of the native media player. That page found that a canvas can restyle the native controls and cannot reach any one of them. This page asks what a canvas could do if media controls were ordinary elements with named parts and states, whether the state of any element can drive an effect through CSS alone, whether drawElementImage() takes a pseudo-element or a part, and whether the composed picture can be sent to another screen.

Controls as a custom elementStates through :has()A pseudo-element as a pictureCasting the canvas

Media controls as a custom element with parts and states

<media-bar> is a mock of customisable media controls: a play button, a timeline, a time and a sound button in an open shadow tree, each with a part name, and custom states for playing and muted. Press Play. The film takes its colour back, because a CSS rule reads media-bar:state(playing). Then tick the box: the canvas stops using the element's layout and draws each part where it wants it, and each part still takes input where it is drawn.

The glass behind the controls is the film drawn a second time with a blur, inside the box of the control. With the box ticked there is no bar: the play button is a part of the shadow tree drawn at more than twice its size in the middle of the film, and the timeline is stretched to the width of the canvas. The component's author made that possible by putting drawable on the parts. A page cannot do it for a part it does not own.

State pseudo-classes that drive an effect through :has()

Tick Lamp. Open the opening hours. Press Save with the email field empty, or type something that is not an address and leave the field. Press Help. Each of the four changes how the card is drawn, and the script has no listener on any of the four elements: a CSS rule for each state sets a number on the canvas.

Opening hours

Monday to Friday, 9 to 5. Saturday, 10 to 2.
The lamp, the opening hours and the email field are in the canvas. This popover is not: it is a sibling of the canvas. Tap outside it to close it.

The numbers have the names that Shader CSS uses for its uniforms. Here a 2D paint handler reads them, so the same rules could drive a shader. A state that belongs to an element outside the canvas works the same way, because :has() is written on an ancestor of both.

A pseudo-element as a picture of its own

The proposal under test: drawElementImage() that takes a pseudo-element or a ::part(), so that a canvas could draw the quotation mark of this quote apart from its text. The line under the canvas says what the browser did with that call. The drawing shows the way round it, which needs the page to know where the pseudo-element's box is.

The mark at the start of this quote is not an element. It is a ::before box. The parts of the native player are out of reach in the same way.From this page

A part of an open shadow tree is different: it is an element, and the first demo draws four of them. What is missing is a way to name a box that is not an element, or an element in a tree the page cannot open.

Show the code

  2. Hand the pseudo-element to drawElementImage().
  3. The way round it: two clipped draws of the whole element.
  4. Styles. The mark has a fixed box.

Casting the composed canvas

The first canvas on this page, film and controls together, as a stream for another screen. Three routes are tried. The Remote Playback API is asked to play a <video> that shows the stream. The Presentation API is asked to open a receiver page on a second screen. The third route opens the same receiver page in a tab, which works with one device: press Play in the first demo, open the receiver, and come back here.

Open the receiver in a tab

A receiver page gets messages and no media, so the stream travels over WebRTC and the Presentation connection, or the BroadcastChannel, carries only the offer and the answer. The controls in the stream are pixels: the receiver cannot press Play.

How it works

  • Custom states are selectors. <media-bar> adds and removes names in ElementInternals.states from the video's events. A rule on the canvas, :has(media-bar:state(playing)), sets --fx-amount, and a transition on the canvas eases it.
  • The canvas reads the numbers. A change of a custom property raises no paint event. The canvas listens for transitionrun and transitionend on itself and asks for a frame at a time between them. When no transition runs, nothing runs.
  • Parts as pictures. drawElementImage() takes any element that has the drawable attribute and is a descendant of the canvas, and an element in an open shadow tree of a canvas child counts. The component sets the attribute on its parts when it has the lift attribute.
  • Pseudo-elements. There is no call that takes one, so the mark is drawn by clipping a draw of its whole element to the mark's box.
  • Casting. canvas.captureStream() gives a video track of the drawn canvas. The sender adds it to an RTCPeerConnection and exchanges one offer and one answer with the receiver.

Live checks

The checks wait for a tap. Each builds its own small canvas in a corner of the window, and none of them touches the demos above. :user-invalid is not checked here, because it needs real input: the tool script types into the field.

Findings

Measured in headless Chromium 157 on 2026-11-21. Not yet run on a phone.

  • Media controls built as a custom element can be drawn part by part. An element in an open shadow tree of a canvas child is drawn as its own picture by drawElementImage() when it has the drawable attribute. The play button was drawn at 2.2 times its size and the timeline stretched to 335 px, and a touch on each reached the part where it was drawn: the play part's hit region was more than 55 px tall, and a tap at three quarters of the stretched timeline moved the film to 7.7 s of 10.
  • A part without drawable cannot be drawn. The call threw InvalidStateError: descendants passed to drawElementImage() must have the attribute. Only the component's author can add it, so this does not help with the native controls or with a closed tree.
  • drawElementImage() does not take a pseudo-element. Element.pseudo('::before') returns a CSSPseudoElement in this browser, and passing it threw TypeError. So did a ShadowRoot. The quotation mark is drawn apart by clipping a draw of the whole quote to a box whose place the style sheet fixes. A pseudo-element with no fixed box could not be found this way.
  • Custom states work as inputs to an effect. canvas:has(media-bar:state(playing)) set --fx-amount to 1 while the fixture video played and back to 0 after pause, with no listener outside the component.
  • :checked, details:open, :user-invalid and :popover-open each drove a number through :has(). The first three belong to elements drawn in the canvas. The popover is a sibling of the canvas, and its rule is written on their common ancestor. :user-invalid matched after text that is not an address was typed and the field was left, and after Save was pressed with the field empty.
  • A transition of a registered custom property raises no paint. It raised one transitionrun and one transitionend on the canvas and 0 paint events in 0.5 s, with the number at 0.44 after 150 ms of 300. The canvas asks for frames between the two events and for none afterwards.
  • The composed canvas can be sent as a stream. captureStream() on the drawable canvas gave one video track, and the film with its controls arrived in the receiver page in a second tab at 378 by 288 over WebRTC, with a BroadcastChannel carrying the offer and the answer. The controls in the stream are pixels.
  • No cast device was available to the test browser. Remote Playback reported that no device is available for a video that shows the canvas stream, and prompt() was rejected with NotAllowedError. PresentationRequest.getAvailability() gave false and start() was rejected with NotFoundError: no screens found. The Presentation route of the receiver page has not run.
  • Not verified: everything on a phone, and both cast routes on a network with a Chromecast or a second screen. Whether Remote Playback offers a device at all for a video whose source is a MediaStream is not known. In one run the frame in the receiver tab showed the glass boxes without the play, time and timeline parts while the sending tab was in the background. In a single tab the stream matched the canvas.
